meta.blurb: Marguerite Gautier wears white camellias twenty-five days a month and red ones for the other five, and nobody in Paris knows why. When a poor young man truly loves her, she dares to dream of a quiet life, until his father calls.
meta.bible: Marguerite Gautier: the Lady of the Camellias, a famous, beautiful young woman of Paris who is seriously ill with a weak chest; generous, quick to laugh and secretly lonely. Camellia: her flower; she carries white camellias twenty-five days of each month and red camellias for five. Armand Duval: a young man of a good family with a small income; honest, passionate and jealous. Monsieur Duval: Armand's father, a respectable official of the tax office; stern but not unkind. Armand's sister: a young woman about to be married. Prudence Duvernoy: Marguerite's neighbour, a dressmaker and go-between; greedy and talkative. Julie Duprat: Marguerite's friend who stays with her at the end and keeps her diary. Nanine: Marguerite's loyal maid. Gaston R: Armand's cheerful friend. Olympe: a lively friend of Marguerite who gives a ball. Count de G: a rich man who paid for Marguerite's life in Paris. Baron de Varville: Marguerite's rich protector in the later part of the story, who challenges Armand to a duel. The Duke: a very old man who treats Marguerite like a lost daughter. The narrator: a Parisian who buys a book at the auction and hears the story from Armand. Places: Paris; the Rue d'Antin, where Marguerite lived; the Champs-Elysees, the long avenue where she drove in her carriage; the Opera, the Variety theatre and the Opera-Comique; Bougival, a village near Paris on the river; Montmartre, the cemetery where she is buried; Toulon and Alexandria, where Armand travels; Marseille. Fixed facts: the book is Manon Lescaut and its inscription reads Manon to Marguerite, Humility, signed Armand Duval; the story takes place in Paris in the 1840s and Marguerite dies in the winter of 1847; the auction of her belongings is held in March. Voice and tone: tender, sad and honest; the narrator refuses to judge Marguerite and asks the reader to be kind.

B1B2: In March 1847, a Parisian saw a notice on a wall announcing that everything in a flat on the Rue d'Antin would be sold. The owner, a woman named Marguerite Gautier, had died, and he wanted to see the flat before the sale.
The flat was full of beautiful things, with silk curtains, gold clocks and large mirrors. Elegant ladies walked from room to room, whispering about the woman who had owned it all.
He remembered seeing Marguerite many times in her carriage on the Champs-Elysees, and in her box at the theatre. She was tall and graceful, and she carried a bunch of camellias wherever she went.
For twenty-five days of every month, Marguerite carried white camellias, and for five days she carried red ones. Nobody in Paris ever found out why, and it was only one of her many mysteries.
At the auction, the narrator bought an old copy of the book Manon Lescaut, because it was cheap. On the first page he found words in ink: Manon to Marguerite, Humility, signed Armand Duval.
Some weeks later, a pale young man came to the narrator's door and said his name was Armand Duval. He asked for the book with such sadness that the narrator gave it to him at once.
Armand visited the grave of Marguerite in the cemetery at Montmartre, and the sight made him very ill. The narrator took him home and cared for him until his fever went down.
When Armand felt strong enough, he decided to tell the narrator everything. He handed him some papers and said that the story was a sad one, but that it was true.
Armand said that he first saw Marguerite at the door of a shop on a Paris street. She was so beautiful that he stopped and stared, and he could not forget her face afterwards.
At the theatre, Armand's friend Gaston told him that the beautiful woman in the box was Marguerite Gautier. Armand watched her laugh and talk all evening, and he knew that he was in love.
Prudence Duvernoy was a neighbour and friend of Marguerite, and she knew Armand's friend Gaston. She invited both young men to dinner at her house, and Marguerite was also asked to come.
At dinner, Marguerite was lively and charming, and she made everyone laugh. Then she began to cough so badly that she had to leave the table and go into the next room.

Armand followed Marguerite into the next room and told her that he was worried about her health. She was surprised, and she told him that he should not care, because she was ill and would not live long.
Marguerite teased Armand and asked whether he was in love with her. He answered that he had loved her for two years, ever since he saw her at the door of a shop.
Marguerite gave Armand a camellia and told him he could come back to see her when it faded. He took it home, watched it carefully and was overjoyed when it wilted the next morning.
When Armand returned, Marguerite told him honestly that her life cost a great deal of money. Rich men paid for her flat, her carriage and her jewels, and she could not live without them.
Marguerite told him that she had been a poor girl from the country, who came to Paris to find work. She had learned fine manners and soon found herself in a life she had not really chosen.
Marguerite told Armand about an old Duke who treated her like the daughter he had lost, and who gave her money out of kindness. She also told him about Count de G, who paid many of her bills.
Marguerite said that she was tired of Paris and wished to live quietly in the country. They found a little house at Bougival, near the river, and moved there together in the early summer.
In the country, Marguerite grew stronger and happier, and her cough became less severe. She read, walked by the river and gardened, and she soon lost her taste for the parties of Paris.

Armand discovered, by chance, that Marguerite had been selling her jewels, her horses and her carriage to pay for their life in the country. He was ashamed that he had not noticed, and he decided to pay her debts himself.
Armand decided to ask for the money that his mother had left him. He wrote to the man who looked after it and travelled to Paris to arrange everything.
In Paris, Armand found several letters from his father, who wanted to see him urgently. Armand went to his father's address, but his father was out, and he did not wait.
While Armand was still away, an elderly gentleman called at the house in Bougival. It was Monsieur Duval, Armand's father, and he had come to speak with Marguerite alone.
Monsieur Duval said that Armand's sister was about to be married to a good man. If the scandal about Armand and Marguerite continued, the husband's family would end the marriage.
Marguerite wept for a long time, but at last she agreed to leave Armand for the sake of his sister. She asked Monsieur Duval not to tell him the real reason, and he promised.
When Armand came home, Marguerite was strangely sad and tender, and she held him tightly. He asked what was wrong, and she said that it was nothing, only that she loved him very much.
Marguerite told Armand to go and see his father, and she kissed him goodbye. As soon as he had gone, she left the house in Bougival and went back to Paris.
Soon after, Armand received a short letter from Marguerite. She wrote that she had gone back to her old life and her old friends, and she said goodbye.
Armand's father took him home to the family house in the country and tried to comfort him. But Armand could only think of Marguerite, and after some days he said that he must return to Paris.
In Paris, Armand went to a ball given by Marguerite's friend Olympe. He saw Marguerite there with a new protector, Baron de Varville, and he felt a hot and bitter anger.
Armand sat down at a card table and played against the Baron. He won a great deal of money, and Marguerite begged him with her eyes to stop, but he did not look at her.
Marguerite took Armand aside and begged him to go home before there was trouble. She said that she had sworn a promise she could not break, but she would not tell him what it was.
Armand, blind with anger, threw his winnings at Marguerite's feet in front of the whole room. He said that he was paying what he owed her, and Marguerite fainted.
The next day, the Baron challenged Armand to a duel. They fought with swords, and Armand wounded the Baron lightly, so the Baron was soon well again.
Armand was so ashamed that he sent Marguerite a copy of Manon Lescaut, with a note that said he was humble. Then he left Paris and travelled far away, because he could not bear to stay.
Meanwhile, in Paris, Marguerite became sicker and sicker through the winter. Her old friends visited less and less, and her debts grew, so that soon she was almost alone.

A friend named Julie Duprat stayed with Marguerite and cared for her through the long winter. Later, Julie wrote an account of Marguerite's last weeks for Armand, and she included the diary that Marguerite had kept.
While travelling, Armand heard that Marguerite was seriously ill. He set out for Paris at once, but when he arrived, he learned that she had already died, only a few days before.
Armand read Marguerite's diary, and in it he learned of her promise to his father. She had given him up on purpose, to save his sister, and she had never stopped loving him.
In her diary, Marguerite wrote about her loneliness and her illness. She wrote that she missed Armand every day, and that she wished to see him once more before she died.
In her last days, Marguerite was cared for by Julie and her maid, Nanine, who never left her side. Marguerite spoke often of Armand, and she held the book Manon Lescaut in her hands.
Marguerite died quietly one morning in the winter, with a little smile on her face. Julie and Nanine said later that she looked calm and as if she had at last been forgiven.
Only a few people came to Marguerite's funeral at Montmartre. The old Duke wept, and Julie and Nanine laid white camellias on the coffin, as she would have wished.
Armand knelt at Marguerite's grave and asked for her forgiveness. He told her that he understood everything now, and he placed a white camellia on the stone.
Armand's father wrote to him with great sorrow, and said that he was sorry for what he had done. Armand's sister married the man she loved, and the whole family was happy except Armand.
When Armand finished his story, he thanked the narrator for listening. He said that it was a great relief to tell it, and that he felt a little calmer than before.
After Armand had gone, the narrator sat for a long time with the book and the letters. He thought about the story, and he decided that he must write it down for others to read.
The narrator wrote that he did not judge Marguerite, and that he hoped the reader would not either. She had loved truly and given up everything for the one she loved, and that was worth remembering.

In the end, the story closes on a quiet grave at Montmartre, where someone had left a single white camellia. It is a sign that Marguerite's love is not forgotten, and the narrator hopes it never will be.
C1C2: In March 1847, a Parisian reading the notices on a street wall found that the contents of a flat in the Rue d'Antin were to be sold after the death of their owner, Marguerite Gautier. He had known her only by sight, as everyone in Paris had, but the notice stirred his curiosity so strongly that he decided to visit the flat before the sale began. He was not yet aware, as he turned away from the wall, that he had just taken the first step into a long and sorrowful story.

The flat was filled with beautiful objects, from silk curtains and gilded clocks to rare china and heavy mirrors, and elegant ladies, some of whom had known the dead woman well, walked from room to room whispering her name. The narrator moved among them in silence, struck by how much beauty had been gathered in one place by one young person. Everything in those rooms seemed to wait patiently for a mistress who would never come back to enjoy it, and the silence was strange.

The narrator remembered seeing Marguerite on the Champs-Elysees in her elegant carriage and, in the evenings, in her box at the theatre, tall, graceful and always richly dressed. Whatever the hour, she carried a bunch of camellias, and it was by this one habit that all Paris knew her and named her. He had never spoken to her in all those years, but he had never really forgotten her either, and he could not say why.

For twenty-five days of every month Marguerite carried white camellias, and for the remaining five she carried red ones, and no one in Paris could explain the reason for the change. It added to her air of mystery, and it gave her the name by which she was remembered, the Lady of the Camellias. The narrator found, as he left the flat and walked home through the grey streets, that he was still thinking about those flowers.

At the sale, in a room filled with shouting and rustling gowns, the narrator bought for a small price a copy of the novel Manon Lescaut, simply because he wanted a little souvenir of the woman. Opening it later at home, he found on the first page a few words in ink, Manon to Marguerite, Humility, signed by a certain Armand Duval. The little phrase touched him more deeply than he could have said, and he wondered who Armand Duval was and what had happened between them.

Some weeks later a pale young man called at the narrator's door and said that his name was Armand Duval, and that he had only just returned from a long journey. He asked to see the book, and when he recognised his own writing, tears ran down his face, and the narrator, deeply moved, put it into his hands without a word. He explained, in a voice full of pain, that he had come back to Paris too late and that he had no other keepsake of her.

Armand went to the cemetery at Montmartre to see Marguerite's grave, and the sight of it shook him so deeply that he fell ill with fever that same evening. The narrator, who had become attached to the sad young man, nursed him for weeks, and the two grew to trust each other as only strangers in trouble can. It was in that quiet sickroom, during the long evenings of his recovery, that Armand finally began to speak about the past.

When he was strong enough to talk at length, Armand decided to tell the narrator everything and gave him a bundle of letters and papers to keep beside the story. He said that he wished it to be told truly, so that Marguerite should not be remembered only for the foolish things the world said about her. The narrator promised to listen with an open mind and a kind heart, and to judge no one until he had heard the end.

Armand said that he first saw Marguerite going into a fashionable shop on a Paris street, years before they were ever introduced. She was so lovely that he stopped and stared like a schoolboy, and for the rest of that day, and for many days afterwards, he could scarcely think of anything else. He did not yet know her name, and he did not dare to ask a single question about her, though he looked for her face in every crowd.

At the theatre one evening, Armand's friend Gaston pointed out a woman in a private box and told him that this was the famous Marguerite Gautier, whom half Paris admired and the other half gossiped about. Armand watched her laughing and chatting through the whole play, and he knew with a dull certainty that he was lost. He had no idea how a poor young man like himself could ever approach such a famous woman, but he decided that he would try.

Prudence Duvernoy, a talkative dressmaker who lived near Marguerite and could never resist an introduction, invited Armand and Gaston to dinner at her house and arranged for Marguerite to be there too. Armand accepted with a heart that beat too fast, and he spent the whole afternoon trying to decide what he would say to her. In the end, when the moment came, he was so nervous that he said almost nothing at all, and he was sure that she thought him stupid.

At dinner Marguerite was lively, witty and charming, and she made the whole table laugh with her stories and her teasing. Then, quite without warning, she began to cough, a painful, tearing cough that she tried to hide behind a smile, and she hurried out of the room with her handkerchief to her lips. Everyone at the table fell silent in embarrassment, and Armand, almost without thinking and against every rule of good manners, rose and followed her out of the room.

Armand found her in the next room, pale and breathing with difficulty, and told her gently that he was troubled by her cough and that she should take care of herself. Marguerite looked at him with surprise, for nobody had spoken to her so kindly in a long time, and she told him that he should not waste his feelings on someone who would not live long. She laughed lightly as she said it, but there were tears in her eyes, and he understood that the laugh was only a shield.

Marguerite, who was accustomed to compliments, teased him and asked whether he was perhaps a little in love with her already. He answered her with such simple earnestness that he had loved her for two years, ever since the day he saw her at a shop door, that she stopped laughing and looked at him for a long moment. It was perhaps the first time in many years that anyone had spoken to her in such a simple and honest way, and it moved her deeply.

Marguerite gave Armand a camellia from her bunch and told him, in a half-joking tone, that he might come back and see her when the flower had faded. He took it home like a treasure, watched it all night, and was overjoyed to see that by the next morning it was already wilting, which meant that he could return that very day. Nobody in all of Paris could have been happier about a dying flower than that young man, who counted the hours until he could knock at her door.

When Armand returned, Marguerite told him honestly that her way of life was expensive, and that her flat, her carriage and her jewels were paid for by rich men who admired her. She said it without shame and without pride, as a plain fact, and she warned him that he, with his small income, could never afford to take their place. Armand, who loved her far too much to be sensible, said that he did not care what it cost or what anyone thought of him.

Marguerite told Armand the story of her life, that she had been a poor country girl who came to Paris to look for work, with nothing but a plain dress and a good heart. She had learned fine manners quickly, and men had noticed her, and before she understood what was happening she had been carried into a life she had never truly chosen. She said it quietly, looking down at her hands, as though she were describing the life of another woman whom she barely knew.

Marguerite told Armand about an old Duke who treated her like a lost daughter, and about Count de G, a younger and wealthier man who paid many of her larger bills. Armand listened with a jealousy that he could not hide, though he knew that he had no right to feel it. She watched him kindly and did not laugh at all, because she knew well enough how it felt to be hurt by a feeling you cannot control.

One day Marguerite said that she was weary of Paris and its noise, and that she wished more than anything to live quietly in the country, with Armand beside her. They found a little house at Bougival, near the river and surrounded by trees, and moved there together in the early summer, leaving the gossips behind. It was the first time in years that she had really thought about the future with any hope, and the thought made her whole face shine.

In the country, Marguerite grew stronger and happier week by week, and her cough eased until it almost disappeared. She read, walked by the river and tended her flowers, and the glittering parties of Paris, which had once seemed so necessary, began to seem as distant as a half-forgotten dream. Armand, watching her from the garden bench, believed that he had never been happier in his whole life, and that nothing could possibly spoil it.

By chance, Armand discovered that Marguerite had been quietly selling her jewels, her horses and even her carriage in order to pay for their life in the country, and that she had said nothing about it to him. He was ashamed that he had not noticed, and he declared that he would take on her debts himself and pay them, whatever it cost him. She tried gently to dissuade him, saying that the sacrifice was hers to make, but he was young and stubborn and would not listen.

Armand decided to claim the share of the property that his late mother had left him, and he wrote to the family lawyer to arrange it, then travelled to Paris to sign the papers. He meant to put every penny of it towards Marguerite's debts, and he did not stop to ask what his father might think of such a plan. For the first time in his life he felt like a real man with a responsibility, and he walked down the road with his head held high.

In Paris, Armand found several letters from his father waiting for him, each more anxious than the last, and he guessed that someone had told him of Marguerite. He called at his father's address, but the old man was out, and Armand, impatient to return to Bougival, did not stay to wait for him. He left a short note instead, and that one careless act, which seemed so small at the time, was to change everything in his life.

While Armand was still in Paris, an elderly and rather stern gentleman called at the little house in Bougival and asked, with perfect courtesy, to speak with Marguerite alone. It was Monsieur Duval, Armand's father, and Marguerite, who had been warned of his visit by a nervous servant, received him in the garden with a pale face and a straight back. She was ready for angry words and insults, for she had heard them before, but she was not at all ready for his gentleness.

Monsieur Duval explained, without anger, that Armand's young sister was about to be married to an excellent man, and that the groom's family would withdraw its consent if the scandal about her brother went on. He did not insult Marguerite or call her names, and he asked her only whether she could sacrifice her own happiness for the sake of another girl's future. The question fell on her heart like a stone, and she sat very still for a moment before she could trust herself to answer.

Marguerite wept for a long time, and Monsieur Duval, who was not a hard man, did not hurry her. At last she agreed to leave Armand for his sister's sake, on one condition: that his father would never tell him why, since he would hate her less if he thought she had left him for money. Monsieur Duval gave his word as an honest man, and he thanked her with a tenderness that she remembered for the rest of her short life.

When Armand came home, Marguerite was strangely sad and gentle, and she held him tightly in her arms as though she was afraid he might vanish. He asked her what was wrong, and she answered that it was nothing, only that she loved him very much and wished him to remember it always. He kissed her and promised that he would remember it always, and, because he was young and happy, he never suspected what she was preparing in secret.

The next day she urged him to go and see his father, who was waiting in a nearby village, and she kissed him goodbye with a long and trembling embrace. The moment he had gone, she packed a small bag, left the house at Bougival and set out for Paris, and she did not look back. Nanine, her loyal maid, who stood crying in the doorway, was the only witness to the leaving, and she never forgot the sight.

Soon after, a servant brought Armand a short, cold letter in Marguerite's hand, saying that she had gone back to her former life, to her old friends and her old comforts, and wishing him goodbye. He read it three times with growing disbelief, then fell into a chair, and the whole world seemed to turn dark. It was the cruellest hour of his young life, and for many years afterwards he could not recall it without a shudder.

Armand's father took him home to the family house in the country and tried to console him with gentle words and quiet walks. But Armand could think only of Marguerite and her betrayal, and after a few days he announced that he must return to Paris, to see her once more and to make her suffer as he had suffered. His father, who alone knew the truth of what Marguerite had done, said nothing, because he had given her his word of honour.

In Paris, Armand attended a ball given by Olympe, a friend of Marguerite's, and there he saw her on the arm of a new and wealthy protector, Baron de Varville. She looked pale and tired beneath her smile, but Armand, blinded by his own pain, noticed nothing except that she seemed to have forgotten him. A hot and bitter anger rose in him, and he felt that he could not rest until he had hurt her as she had hurt him.

Armand sat down at the card table to play against the Baron, and for hours he won with a kind of cold fury, until a pile of money lay in front of him. Marguerite, who stood nearby, begged him with her eyes to stop, but he refused to look at her, and the Baron, white with anger, said nothing. Everyone gathered around the table sensed that something dreadful was about to happen, and the music in the next room seemed to grow thin.

Marguerite took Armand aside and begged him in a whisper to leave the ball before there was trouble, because the Baron was dangerous and she feared for him. She told him that she had sworn a promise that she could never break, but she would not say what it was, and her refusal only fed his anger. He told her coldly that he would go only if she went with him that very minute, and she, trapped by her promise, could only shake her head.

Blind with anger, Armand took the money he had won, called out that he wished to pay what he owed her, and threw it at her feet in front of the whole room. Marguerite gave a low cry and fainted, and the guests gasped in shocked silence, and Armand, in that moment, realised at last what he had done. The cruelty of the act could never be taken back, and every guest who saw it understood that something between them had been destroyed.

The next day the Baron sent his friends to challenge Armand to a duel, and the two men met at dawn with swords in a quiet field outside Paris. Armand, who had more youth and less skill, wounded the Baron lightly in the arm, and the Baron recovered within a few weeks. Armand felt neither pride nor relief at the result, only a great and growing shame that stayed with him through the whole of the following week.

Armand, tormented by shame, sent Marguerite a copy of the book Manon Lescaut with a few lines inside that spoke of his humility and sorrow, and then, without waiting for any answer, he left Paris. He travelled for months through distant lands, telling himself that he was forgetting her, while the pain went with him wherever he went. It was, as he said himself many years later, the worst and most foolish mistake of his whole life, and he never fully forgave himself.

In Paris, Marguerite's health failed rapidly through that winter, and the friends who had gathered round her in her splendour grew fewer and fewer. Her debts multiplied, her admirers drifted away, and the luxuries that had once surrounded her were taken one by one, until only a faithful few remained at her side. She never once spoke ill of Armand, even in her weakest hours, and she kept his letters close at hand until the end.

A friend named Julie Duprat, who had known Marguerite for years, stayed with her through the long winter, and she watched over her with patience and affection when the others had gone. Later she set down an account of those last weeks for Armand, and she added a diary that Marguerite herself had kept in the evenings. It was this record, written with such care and love, that he read when he finally came back to Paris and knew that she was gone.

While travelling abroad, Armand received a letter telling him that Marguerite was seriously ill, and he set out for Paris at once, travelling day and night without rest. When he arrived, he was told that she had died only a few days before and that she had been buried in the cemetery at Montmartre. He stood in the empty street for a long time, unable to move or speak, while carriages passed him and the city went on as before.

Armand read the diary slowly by lamplight, and in it he found at last the truth about her promise to his father, which she had kept even when it ruined her. She had given him up on purpose, to save his sister's future, and she had written without a word of complaint that she had never for one day stopped loving him. He wept as he had never wept before, and for the first time he understood how completely he had misjudged her.

In her diary, Marguerite described her loneliness and her illness with a simple honesty, and she wrote that she missed Armand each day and hoped that he would come back before the end. She did not blame him for his cruelty, and she wrote that she understood how much he had suffered, and that she forgave everything. Armand, reading it by the lamp, could hardly see the page through his tears, and he had to stop again and again to compose himself.

In her last days, Marguerite was looked after by Julie and by her loyal maid, Nanine, who never left her side and who spoke to her softly through the long nights. She spoke often of Armand, and she held the copy of Manon Lescaut that he had sent her, reading again the words he had written inside. She was waiting, right to the end, for a knock at the door that never came, and her friends could not bear to tell her it would not.

Marguerite died quietly one morning in the winter of 1847, with a little smile on her lips and her friends beside her. Julie and Nanine said afterwards that she had looked calm at the end, as if she had at last been forgiven for all the wrong she had never really done. It was, they said, a gentle death, free of fear and pain, and the room was very still for a long time afterwards.

Only a handful of mourners followed Marguerite's coffin up the hill to the cemetery at Montmartre, and among them the old Duke, who wept openly, and Julie and Nanine, who carried white camellias to lay on her grave. Those who had once crowded her rooms and drunk her wine were nowhere to be seen, and she was left to the few who had loved her truly. It was a modest end for a famous woman, and it showed how few of those who had enjoyed her company had truly cared for her.

Armand went to Marguerite's grave and knelt there in the cold light, and he asked her forgiveness aloud, though he knew that no one could hear him. He told her that he understood everything at last, that he knew what she had given up for him and for his family, and he laid a white camellia on the stone. For the first time since his return, he wept without anger, and the tears seemed to wash away a little of his bitterness.

Armand's father wrote to him in a trembling hand, saying that he had judged Marguerite wrongly and that he deeply regretted the part he had played in her sorrow. Armand's sister married the man she loved and was very happy, and the family held a quiet celebration, but Armand, who knew what it had cost, could not join in the joy. He wished only that Marguerite, who had made it all possible, could have seen it, and he said so to anyone who would listen.

When Armand had finished his story, he thanked the narrator for his patience and said that to tell it, at last, had given him more relief than anything else in a year. He asked only that it should be remembered truly, as the story of a woman who had loved more than she was ever given credit for. The narrator, who was deeply moved by the request, promised that he would tell the story exactly as it had been told to him.

After Armand had gone, the narrator sat for a long time with the book and the bundle of letters in front of him, thinking over everything he had heard. He had come to feel that the story ought not to be lost, and that anyone who read it with an open heart might understand Marguerite better than the world had. He took a clean sheet of paper, dipped his pen into the ink, and began to write the first words of the story you have just read.

The narrator wrote that he could not judge Marguerite, and that he hoped no reader would be too quick to do so either. She had been sold a life she did not choose, she had loved truly when the chance came, and she had given up everything she had won in order to protect someone else. That, he thought, was worth far more than all the easy opinions of a world that had never troubled to know her.

The story ends where it began, in Paris, with a quiet grave at Montmartre on which someone has left a single white camellia, fresh and unfaded. It is a sign that Marguerite's love is not forgotten, and the narrator, who never knew her in life, hopes that anyone who reads her story will remember it a little longer. The flower, white for most of the month, stands for what she most truly was.
